title: Maya's $5K card - the $100/month trap (record card debt)
caption: Her $5,000 credit card balance was on track to cost her almost $12K. Here's the math.

lines.text: Her five thousand dollar credit card balance is on track to cost her almost twelve thousand.
And she's not alone. Americans now owe a record one point two nine trillion dollars on credit cards.

visual.label: US credit card debt, a new record

lines.text: That's from the New York Fed's newest report, out this month.
So meet Maya. She's twenty four.
She has five thousand dollars on a card charging about twenty one percent.
Which is pretty much the average rate the Fed reports right now.
Maya pays one hundred dollars a month. Feels responsible, right?
Here's the catch. About eighty seven dollars of that first payment is just interest.
So her balance barely moves.
At a hundred a month, she's paying that card for ten whole years.
And she hands over almost seven thousand dollars in interest alone.
More than the stuff she actually bought.

visual.text: wait... i paid more in interest than i actually spent??

lines.text: Now, same card, same balance. What if she pays two fifty a month instead?
She's done in about two years.
And the interest drops to around twelve hundred dollars.
An extra hundred and fifty a month kept almost fifty eight hundred dollars in her pocket.
That's why card debt keeps hitting records. Interest stacks up faster than most people pay it down.
A few moves people use to get out faster. Paying more than the minimum. Hitting the highest rate card first. Or calling and asking for a lower rate.
Because a five thousand dollar balance should never turn into twelve.
So what's the APR on your card? Check it, and drop it in the comments.

claims.claim: US credit card balances hit a record ~$1.29 trillion ($1.285T) in Q3 2026
Average credit card rate about 21% (Fed G.19: 21.19% all accounts, 22.36% accounts assessed interest)
$5,000 at 21% APR: first month's interest $87.50; $100/mo takes 120 months and $6,986 interest (total ~$11,986); $250/mo takes 25 months and $1,208 interest; difference $5,778
